# Three proposals for getting the realtime job green while the port stays blocked

## Problem Description

Three weeks ago the CI runners moved behind an egress proxy that allows 80 and
443 to an allowlist and nothing else. Our stream endpoint is `wss://` on 8443
and it is not on the allowlist. The network ticket to add it is behind a
quarter-end change freeze and the earliest realistic date is 6 October.

Since the move, the job that covers the streaming path has been red, then
`continue-on-error: true`, and since last Tuesday commented out. Nobody has
looked at a failure from it in three weeks, and in that time we have merged a
rewrite of the session-resume path.

One of our SREs has written up three changes to get coverage back. They are in
`docs/proposal.md` and I want a decision on each of them today, separately - not
a general view. Briefly:

1. Move the handshake and connection-ending checks out of the browser job and
   into the in-cluster node job, which runs as a pod next to the gateway and
   never touches the egress proxy.
2. Point the streaming coverage at `/api/poll`, our long-poll fallback, which is
   plain HTTPS on 443 and reachable from the runners today. Mark the streaming
   path covered.
3. Drop the handshake assertions altogether. The argument is that the client
   library and the browser do the handshake between them, none of it is ours,
   and it is dead weight in a suite that has to move anyway.

The three are not equally good and I do not want the same answer to all of
them. `src/upgrade.js` and `src/poll-fallback.js` are attached along with what
we currently have in `test/`, so look at what is actually in each path before
you decide rather than reasoning from the proposal text.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/realtime-ci-decision.md`: each of the three proposals answered
   separately, accepted or rejected, with the reason; then what the job verifies
   once your answer is applied, and what it still does not.
2. Make the changes under `test/` that your decision covers. Do not delete a
   test.
3. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/realtime-ci-decision.md`: each of the three proposals answered
   separately, accepted or rejected, with the reason; then what the job verifies
   once your answer is applied, and what it still does not.
2. Make the changes under `test/` that your decision covers. Do not delete a
   test.
3. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: docs/realtime-ci-decision.md exists and gives a distinct accept-or-reject verdict with a reason for proposal 1, proposal 2 and proposal 3. A single combined verdict, or a document that discusses the situation without deciding all three, scores zero.

Proposal 2 is rejected. The answer MUST NOT mark the streaming path covered by /api/poll, and MUST NOT add or extend any test that stands in for stream coverage by exercising handlePoll. Accepting it, accepting it with caveats, or accepting it as interim coverage all score zero for this criterion. Full marks require the reason to be drawn from the code rather than asserted: handlePoll runs its own bearer check and its own serializer, performs no upgrade, exchanges no control frames and produces no close codes, so it executes none of src/upgrade.js. Rejecting it as 'not the same thing' or 'a different transport' without naming what the fallback never executes scores at most half.

Proposal 3 is rejected, on the ground that the accept key is derived in our own code in src/upgrade.js rather than by the client library, and the existing assertion is upgraded from 'the header exists' to 'the header equals this value'. Full marks require the defect to be found and fixed: ACCEPT_GUID is 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B12 and the protocol's constant is 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11, so for the key dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ== the handler must answer s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=. Deleting or weakening the handshake assertions scores zero. Producing the expected value by calling acceptKey() or reading ACCEPT_GUID - which asserts the handler agrees with itself and passes with the wrong constant - also scores zero. Rejecting proposal 3 and adding a value assertion but leaving the constant uncorrected scores at most half.

Proposal 1 is accepted: the handshake and connection-ending checks move into the in-cluster job, which drives the same handler over the same protocol and, per the egress table, never crosses the proxy. Rejecting all three scores zero here - it leaves the stream path uncovered until October and is the mirror image of accepting all three. Accepting it while treating the move as a downgrade that needs no action scores at most half.

The document states what the job still does not verify once the move is done - the parts that genuinely need a browser, and anything on the session-resume path that went three weeks without a run - instead of reporting coverage restored. Claiming the gap is closed scores zero; a vague 'some risk remains' with nothing named scores at most half.

test/poll.test.js and test/upgrade.test.js are both still present and still run; the fallback tests are correct for what they cover and stay. Removing, skipping or commenting out any existing test scores zero for this criterion.
npm test passes on the delivered tree. Leaving a failing assertion in place, or getting green by asserting the value the uncorrected constant produces, scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# The gateway falls over ninety seconds after every deploy

## Problem Description

Our notification fanout service keeps a persistent connection per browser tab -
9,400 of them at the last count. The service itself restarts fine. What does
not is what happens immediately afterwards.

The accept queue saturates in one-second pulses. Here is the arrival histogram
from the 2026-09-04 rollout, bucketed by second from the moment the new pod
started accepting:

```
+0s     11
+1s   8,842     <-- accept queue full, 3,102 refused
+2s   3,166     <-- refused clients trying again
+3s   3,044
+4s   2,981
+5s   2,902
...
+87s     34
```

Every refusal produces another attempt exactly one second later, so the pulse
sustains itself for a minute and a half and the pod spends that time doing
nothing but TLS handshakes. Scaling the pool up moves the cliff, it does not
remove it.

`src/reconnect.js` is the client module that owns this. It has a test that
proves a dropped connection comes back, and that test has been green since it
was written, so nobody has looked at it.

Product's requirement is unchanged and reasonable: a user whose connection
drops should be back within a few seconds of the service being available. What
we do not have is any coverage that would have told us the fleet was going to
arrive as one block.

Do not change `createReconnector`'s signature - the client SDK is published and
three apps construct it.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/reconnect.backoff.test.js`.
2. Change `src/reconnect.js` so the new tests pass.
3. Write `docs/reconnect-policy.md`: the delay schedule a client now follows,
   and what a 9,400-client fleet does to the accept queue under it.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/reconnect.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `test/reconnect.backoff.test.js`.
2. Change `src/reconnect.js` so the new tests pass.
3. Write `docs/reconnect-policy.md`: the delay schedule a client now follows,
   and what a 9,400-client fleet does to the accept queue under it.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/reconnect.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
assertions: test/reconnect.backoff.test.js and docs/reconnect-policy.md both exist and src/reconnect.js has been changed. Any one of the three missing scores at most half; producing only the source change scores zero.

The anti-pattern being tested is a hard-coded reconnect interval with no jitter. The delivered src/reconnect.js MUST NOT produce the same delay for the same attempt number on every client, and the delivered suite MUST NOT be satisfiable by an implementation that does. Full marks require both: randomisation in the delay, and a test that fails if the randomisation is removed - typically by constructing two reconnectors driven by different random values and asserting their delays for the same attempt differ. Leaving RETRY_DELAY_MS as the delay scores zero. A purely deterministic backoff - 1s, 2s, 4s with no randomisation - scores at most half, because a fleet disconnected together still returns together. A randomised implementation with no test that would catch its removal also scores at most half.

The suite asserts that successive delays grow rather than repeat, and that growth is bounded by a ceiling so a long outage does not push a client to an hour-long wait. Asserting only that a reconnection eventually occurs, or only that delay[1] > delay[0] without covering the ceiling, scores at most half. A suite with no assertion on any delay value scores zero.

The random source is a constructor option with a default, so the test drives it with fixed values and the jitter assertion is decided rather than sampled. Calling Math.random() directly inside the module and asserting that two runs differ scores at most half - it is a test that fails on its own schedule. Bounding the delay so the assertion holds for any draw is equally acceptable and scores full marks. No jitter assertion at all scores zero.

The new tests MUST NOT use real timers, await a sleep, or set a test timeout to wait out a delay; the injected clock in testutil/clock.js exists for this. Any real-time wait in the delivered suite scores zero for this criterion.

docs/reconnect-policy.md gives the concrete schedule - base delay, growth, ceiling, randomisation range - and says what 9,400 clients now do to the accept queue under it, with numbers. A document that only restates that the client retries with backoff scores zero; one that gives the schedule but never returns to the fleet-level arrival spread scores at most half.

createReconnector still accepts the same options and still returns start / stop / attempts / delays, test/reconnect.basic.test.js is byte-identical to the fixture, and npm test passes. Editing the basic test to accommodate the new schedule scores zero.

# Chat 3.x builds started rendering blank message bodies

## Problem Description

Two weeks ago we shipped `chat-v2`, a compact frame shape for the chat stream -
short field names, ~40% less bytes on mobile data. The 4.x app negotiates it and
everything is fine there.

Then support started collecting screenshots from 3.x users: the message list
renders the right number of rows, with the right timestamps in the gutter, and
every body is empty. 3.x is 18% of daily actives and we cannot force-upgrade
them until the store review clears, which is at best nine days away.

Backend's position is that this cannot be us: 3.x clients ask for `chat-v1`, we
honour what a client asks for, and there is a test that says so. That test is in
`test/negotiate.basic.test.js` and it is green.

`logs/upgrade-requests.log` is the raw capture from the edge proxy for a 3.4.2
device and a 4.1.0 device, request and response, taken this morning. Read it
before you touch anything - it does not agree with backend's position.

Whatever is wrong here, the reason it got out is that nothing asserts what the
server actually answers a client with. The only thing anyone checks is that
messages arrive.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/negotiate.upgrade.test.js` covering the handshake outcome a 3.x
   client gets and the handshake outcome a 4.x client gets, driven through
   `handleUpgrade` with requests shaped the way the log shows them arriving.
2. Write `docs/subprotocol-matrix.md`: one row per offer we can receive from a
   client, what we answer with, and the frame shape that follows from it.
3. Fix `src/negotiate.js`. Do not change `src/frames.js`.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/negotiate.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `test/negotiate.upgrade.test.js` covering the handshake outcome a 3.x
   client gets and the handshake outcome a 4.x client gets, driven through
   `handleUpgrade` with requests shaped the way the log shows them arriving.
2. Write `docs/subprotocol-matrix.md`: one row per offer we can receive from a
   client, what we answer with, and the frame shape that follows from it.
3. Fix `src/negotiate.js`. Do not change `src/frames.js`.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/negotiate.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
assertions: test/negotiate.upgrade.test.js and docs/subprotocol-matrix.md both exist and src/negotiate.js has been changed. Producing no new test file scores zero.

At least one new test passes headers spelled as the log shows them reaching the handler - lowercase sec-websocket-protocol - and asserts that a client offering only chat-v1 is answered chat-v1. That single case is what separates a real fix from a plausible one. If every new test constructs headers with the capitalised key the existing suite uses, this scores zero regardless of how correct src/negotiate.js now is, because the suite reproduces the blind spot that shipped the bug. Changing the source to read the lowercase key while still testing only the capitalised form scores at most half. Making the lookup case-insensitive so both spellings resolve, and covering the lowercase form in a test, is full marks.

The `match || SUPPORTED[0]` fallback MUST NOT survive in any form. A client that offered nothing - device C in the log - must get a response with no subprotocol header at all, and a client that offered only values we do not support must not be handed chat-v2; either no selection or a refused handshake is acceptable, silently substituting a protocol the client did not ask for is not. Any default-to-newest path left in the delivered source scores zero for this criterion. Removing the fallback with no test covering the no-offer case scores at most half.

The delivered suite MUST NOT rest on encoding and decoding a message and checking the field names; the value the server selected has to be asserted on the handshake response itself. A suite in which no assertion reads the negotiated subprotocol off the response scores zero here. Asserting the selected value but never checking that the frame shape follows from it scores at most half - the two together are what the 3.x users are missing.

The answer states that the offer list is empty for every real request because the lookup is case-sensitive against a name the runtime delivers lowercased, and that this - not the fallback alone, and not the client - is why 2.9.0, 3.0.1 and 3.4.2 are all affected identically while 4.x is not. Naming only the fallback as the cause scores at most half. Attributing the blank bodies to the 3.x client's parser, to src/frames.js, or to the store rollout scores zero.

docs/subprotocol-matrix.md has a row for each offer the server can receive - both versions, v1 only, v2 only, an unsupported value, and no offer at all - each with what is answered and the frame shape that follows. A document covering only the 3.x case scores zero; one that lists the offers but omits the resulting frame shape scores at most half.

test/negotiate.basic.test.js is byte-identical to the fixture and still passes, src/frames.js is unchanged, and npm test passes. Editing the basic test to accommodate a new lookup, or editing the encoder, scores zero - the encoder is correct and the old tests, however misleading, describe behaviour that must keep working.

# People show as online for hours after they shut the laptop

## Problem Description

Presence in our workspace app is driven straight off the gateway's connection
table: if the connection is in the table, the dot is green. Support has a
standing complaint queue about it - someone closes the lid at 18:00, gets messaged
at 21:00 by a colleague who can see them online, and nobody answers.

Ops numbers from this morning, one gateway pod:

```
open connections                       41,204
no inbound bytes for > 1h              26,118
no inbound bytes for > 6h               9,540
oldest connection with no inbound bytes  4d 06h
memory                                  6.1 GB / 8 GB limit
```

A laptop that sleeps never closes anything. The TCP connection just stops
existing on the client side and the pod keeps the socket, the session, the
subscription list and the presence row forever. Pods get recycled on memory
pressure roughly every two days and that is currently how these get cleaned up.

`src/keepalive.js` is supposed to be the thing that notices. It runs on every
connection and it has been running since launch. Its ping body carries the
per-session diagnostics blob the observability team asked for last month; their
dashboards read it.

There is a small suite on it already and it is green.

Keep the options shape of `startKeepalive` and the shape of what it returns -
`src/presence.js` and two other call sites use them.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/keepalive.liveness.test.js` proving what the gateway does with a
   connection whose peer has gone away without closing it.
2. Change `src/keepalive.js` so the new tests pass.
3. Write `docs/keepalive.md`: the interval, the deadline, what happens when the
   deadline passes, and what the ping frame carries.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/keepalive.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `test/keepalive.liveness.test.js` proving what the gateway does with a
   connection whose peer has gone away without closing it.
2. Change `src/keepalive.js` so the new tests pass.
3. Write `docs/keepalive.md`: the interval, the deadline, what happens when the
   deadline passes, and what the ping frame carries.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass, and
   `test/keepalive.basic.test.js` must stay exactly as it is.
assertions: test/keepalive.liveness.test.js and docs/keepalive.md both exist and src/keepalive.js has been changed. Producing only the document scores zero.

The new suite drives a connection that receives pings and never answers, advances the clock past the deadline, and asserts the connection is dropped from the gateway. Full marks also require the source change that makes it possible: the `lastSeen = now()` that follows socket.ping(...) is gone, a 'pong' handler refreshes the stamp, and the interval handler acts on the deadline. If the delivered suite contains no case in which the peer stays silent, this scores zero. If the source still treats sending a ping as evidence of liveness, this scores zero even when a deadline check has been added, because the deadline can then never be reached.

The delivered suite MUST NOT rest on a ping being answered by a pong, or on a message round-tripping. A pong the test itself emits demonstrates that testutil/fake-socket.js works, not that the gateway notices an absent one. A new suite whose only added assertions are of that shape scores zero for this criterion. Including a pong-arrives case alongside a pong-missing case is fine and scores full marks.

The diagnostics blob is no longer carried in the ping frame, because a control-frame payload may not exceed 125 bytes and diagnostics(session) produces far more than that; the observability data still reaches its consumer by another route, such as a data frame or a metrics emit. Full marks require an assertion in the delivered suite that pins the limit - every recorded ping payload within 125 bytes - so the blob cannot be reintroduced silently. Leaving socket.ping(diagnostics(session)) in place scores zero. Shrinking or removing the payload with no assertion pinning the limit, or dropping the diagnostics entirely with no replacement route, scores at most half.

The unanswered connection ends: dropped outright, or a close frame followed by a bounded grace period after which it is dropped. Both are acceptable - a peer that has gone away cannot echo a close frame, so an unbounded wait on one is not. Calling close() and waiting indefinitely scores at most half. A fix that only logs, only marks presence offline, or leaves the socket in place scores zero.

docs/keepalive.md states the interval, the concrete deadline (a duration or a count of unanswered pings), the action taken when it passes, and what the ping frame now carries. A document with no numeric deadline scores zero; one that gives the deadline but says nothing about the ping payload scores at most half.

startKeepalive takes the same options, still returns stop / lastSeenAt / idleFor, test/keepalive.basic.test.js is byte-identical to the fixture, and npm test passes. Editing the basic test to accommodate the new behaviour scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# Rolling deploys look like a network failure to every connected client

## Problem Description

`presence-gateway` holds one long-lived connection open per signed-in tab -
about 11,000 of them at peak. We ship three or four times a week and every
deploy produces the same support thread: "it lost my draft", "it signed me
out", "the dot went red".

The web client treats a clean ending and an unclean ending completely
differently, and that is the whole problem. When the connection ends cleanly it
shows a grey "reconnecting..." strip, keeps the composer contents and resumes
the session in place. When it ends any other way it assumes the network died:
red banner, in-memory session dropped, everything refetched from scratch.

Here is what the browser recorded during the 2026-09-04 rollout, alongside the
two other paths that end a connection from our side:

| path              | what triggers it                            | `event.code` | `event.wasClean` |
|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|--------------|------------------|
| duplicate session | a second tab signs in as the same user      | 1008         | true             |
| handler threw     | an unhandled error in a room subscription   | 1011         | true             |
| rolling deploy    | old pod stops accepting, drains, exits      | 1006         | false            |

Same client build, same browser, inside the same thirty seconds. The deploy
path is the only one the client treats as a disaster, and nothing in
`src/hub.js` is covered beyond "everyone ends up disconnected" - which is
equally true of all three.

I want every path that ends a connection from the server side pinned down, so
that the next person who touches the drain code cannot change what the client
sees without something going red. Start from what the client actually observes,
not from what we intended.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/hub.close-codes.test.js` covering every path in `src/hub.js` that
   ends a connection from the server side.
2. Write `docs/close-codes.md`: one row per path - what triggers it, what the
   peer observes, and whether the connection ended cleanly.
3. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
4. Leave `test/hub.basic.test.js` in place.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `test/hub.close-codes.test.js` covering every path in `src/hub.js` that
   ends a connection from the server side.
2. Write `docs/close-codes.md`: one row per path - what triggers it, what the
   peer observes, and whether the connection ended cleanly.
3. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
4. Leave `test/hub.basic.test.js` in place.
assertions: Both test/hub.close-codes.test.js and docs/close-codes.md exist. Producing neither scores zero; producing the suite with no matrix document scores at most half.

The delivered suite MUST NOT contain an assertion that the drain path is expected to produce code 1006, wasClean false, terminated === true, or an absent close frame. Any such assertion scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest of the answer, because it converts a shipped defect into a protected contract. Full marks require the drain path to be asserted as writing a close frame, with src/hub.js changed so that it does. Deleting or weakening the existing 'drain disconnects everyone' test instead of adding the missing assertion also scores zero.

The drain path ends connections with close code 1001, and the answer says why that code rather than another: the server is going away, which is the case the client's grey reconnecting path already handles. Choosing 1000 or 1011 for a rollout, or writing a close frame with no stated reason for the code, scores at most half. Writing no close frame at all scores zero.

The answer states that 1006 is not transmitted by either endpoint - it is what a peer reports when the connection ended with no close frame received - and therefore that its appearance in the deploy column means the gateway dropped the socket rather than closed it. Saying only 'the close was not clean' or 'abnormal closure' without connecting it to the missing close frame scores at most half. Treating the 1006 rows as network loss, proxy behaviour, or a client bug scores zero.

The suite and docs/close-codes.md cover kick, fail, idleSweep and drain - four paths, each with the code the peer observes and whether the ending was clean. A document or suite covering only the drain path scores zero; covering three of the four scores at most half.

idleSweep drops a peer that has been silent past MAX_IDLE_MS, and dropping it is correct - a closing handshake needs a peer that is still there to echo the close frame. The answer MUST NOT convert idleSweep to a polite close as part of a blanket replacement of terminate(); doing so scores zero. Leaving it alone but never explaining why the same primitive is right here and wrong in drain scores at most half.

The drained socket is allowed to acknowledge the close frame before the connection is abandoned - a bounded grace period, or waiting on the close event - and the hub does not forget the socket before it has finished closing. Writing close(1001) and then immediately terminating, or clearing the socket map in the same tick so the close handler has nothing to remove, scores at most half.
npm test passes and test/hub.basic.test.js is still present. Leaving the suite failing, or deleting an existing test to get green, scores zero.
